The learned Advocate contends that the right to self-determination received judicial recognition in the cases of Namibia and Western Sahara. In support of his contention he quoted the following passage from his book-HUMAN RIGHTS. SELF DETERMI-NATION AND THE RIGHT '10 RESISTANCE : THE CASE STUDY OF HAWAII, 

 "Moreover, in his separate opinion in the Namibia Case, Judge AMM01.111, citing statement by the representative of Pakistan, said that the "right of self-determination is a norm of the nature of just cogens, derogation from which is not permissible under any circumstances". 

 Judge Ammoun also referred to the principle of self-determination in his separate opinion in the Barcelona Traction Case. 

 Relying up-on the above noted observation in the cases cited by him and the pas-sages and Article of the Convention he submit that even if a member of a group is killed, that would amount to genocied. Therefore, if Anup  Chetia; is extradited to India Bangladesh shall be held responsible under Article 111 (b) and 111 (e) of the Convention, The right to life is a peremptory norm of International Law accepted and recognised by the International corn- ' munity of States as a whole from which no derogation is permitted. He further submits that notice is to be taken of the Declaration on the Granting of Independence to Colonial Countries and Peoples (UNGA Res. 1514 xxxx (xv) (1960), and the Declaration on Friendly Relations and 'Co-operation Among-States in accordance with the Charter of the United Nations, GA Res. 2625 (xxv), 25 UNGAOR, Supp. (No.28).  5. Before we enter upon discussion on merit of the case we propose to consider the question of maintainability of this petition. In Dr. Mohiuddin Faruk the petitioner as a public spirited person filed the writ petition for protection of the right to life guaranted under Article 32 of our Constitution to ex-pause the cause of members of the public. The facts of that case are that the petitioner. Dr. Mohiuddin Faruk was the Secretary General of the Bangladesh Environmental Lawyer's Association, shortly called, BELA. The said organisation has been contributing to maintain balance in the field of averment and ecology of Bangladesh. In that writ petition the implementation of Flood Action FAP-20 was impugned on the Ground that such implementation would adversely effect more than a million human lives and natural resources habitat of man and other flora and fauna in the District of Tangail anal the adjacent areawhich aroused wideattention as implementation of the Programme is anti-elvironment and anti-people project. The petitioner further staled in the petition that the BELA conducted investigations at various times from 1992-93 in the FAP-20 areas. He alleged that no proper environmental impact assessment had been under taken in relation to the FAP projects although the European Parliament declared in its resolution of 24 June 1993 that there was urgent need of changing the FAP's classification within the World Bank project scheme from category 'B' to category 'A' requiring full environmental assessment. A group of environmental lawyers possessed of pertinent, bonafide and well recognized expertise contributed in the field of environment and having dedicated and established status moved the writ petition for a judicial review of certain activities under FAP under taken with foreign assistance on the grounds inter alia that implementation of the programme will cause environmental degradation and ecological in balance in the district of Tangail and adjacent areas in violation of the law. The petitioner argued before the High Court Division that he is a person aggrieved as contemplated under Article 102(1) of the Constitution of People's Republic of Bangladesh. The High Court Division, however, negative his contention holding that he is not a "person aggrieved" and summarily rejected the writ petition. The petitioner took an appeal to the Appellate Division. But the Appellate Division held that the petitioner is an aggrieved person. The learned Advocate for the petitioner before us relying upon the referred observation. para 96, of the case of Dr. Mohiuddin Faruk contends that the present petitioner who is also a Secretary-General of the Human Rights Commission of Bangladesh is a "person aggrieved" within the meaning of Article 102(1) of the constitution like the petitioner in Dr. Mohiuddin Faruk as his "heart bleeds" for Anup.Chetia who is expousing the cause of the Assamese people for self-determination. At paragraph 96 of the report the Appellate Division observed: 

 "A person pleading sufficient interest may be able to cross, what is called, the threshold stage on the averments made in the writ. petition but it will always remain open for a prospective respondent to contest the said claim on facts and also to assail the  bonafide or even the appropriateness in a particular case of the petitioner for seeking a relief invoking the Constitutional jurisdiction of the High Court Division under Article 102 of the Constitution. For example standing was denied to the Bangladesh Sangbad Patra Parishad to represent its opulent members, namely the newspaper owners who were 'directly affected by the Wage 'Board Award but even then none of them moved personally, but the Consideration would have been different if any organization representing a weaker section of the Society had come to complain about a breach of any fundamental right of its members or any public wrong done to the members generally in breach of any provision of the constitution or law The Court will have to decide in each, particularly when objection is taken, not only the extent of sufficiency of interest but also the fitness of the person for invoking the discretionary jurisdiction under Article 102 of the Constitution. Ordinarily, it is the affected party which is to come to the Court for remedy. The Court in considering the question of the standing in a particular' case, if the affected party is not before it, will enquire as to why the affected party is not coming before it and if it finds no satisfactory reason for non-appearance of the affected party, it may refuse to entertain the application (Emphasis added). 

 6. As this case is of first impression we are inclined to consider the contention raised at the Bar on merit. Before we examine the decisions and the views expressed in the case relied upon by the learned Advocate for the petitioner we want to examine the law and the Constitutions position obtaining in our country. The learned Advocate relying upon Article.25 of our Constitution con-tended that Anup Chetia, if extradicted to India the Government would violate the mandate of Article 25, The contention on the facts of this case is totally misconceived. Rather the Government can take help of Article 25 for the purpose to extra-diet. Anup Chetia to Indian authority in order to base its international relations on the principle of respect for national sovereignty and equality, non-interference in the internal affairs of other countries. True, that fundamental principle of state policy, here Article 25, cannot be enfourced in by Court nevertheless the fundamental principles of state policy is fundamental to the Government of the Bangladesh, and serve as a tool An interpreting the Constitution and other laws of Bangladesh on the strength of Article .8(2) of the Constitution by the superior Court. Article 25(1)(c) enjoins upon the state to support oppressed people throughout the world waging a just struggle against imperialism, colonialism or racialism. We are afraid to accept the contention that as because Anup Chetia is struggling for "self-determination" for the people of Assam handing over him to India would be violative of Art& 25 of our' Constitution. The struggle in which ULFA and its Secretary-General Anup Chetia is involved is not in our opinion "waging a just struggle against imperialism, colonialism or racialism." The petitioner in this petition states "That Mr. Chetia is the Secretary-General of the liberation Front of Assam (ULFA) the party leading the liberation struggle of the Assamese People." It is difficult for us to view' Liberation struggle of the Assamese People " as" 'struggle against imperialism, colonialism or racialism" the expressions employed in Article 25(1)(c) of the Constitution of People's Republic of Bangladesh. Nor can it be said that right to "self-determination" as canvassed in this petition falls within any of the three expressions Viz, "imperialism", "Colonialism" or "racialism" as used in Article 25(1)(c) in our Constitution. In this context we our-selves inclined to refer to the decision in the case of M. Saleemullah Vs. Government of Bangladesh, 47 D.L.R.218 which one of us is a party, The fact. of that case are that the Government took the decision to participate in the UN -Sponsored Multinational Force to Haiti help maintain public safety and basic Civil( order after restoration of the legitimately elected- Government of Haiti under the UN Security council's Resolution No. 940. The petitioner stated that the Bangladesh Observer also published news under the caption "Ghali asks army rulers to quit-Us aircraft carrier ready to sail for invasion of Haiti, and that the Stale Department announced in Washington that seventeen countries including three NATO allies and Bangladesh have pledged a combined minimum of 1500 troops to assist a US-led invasion of Haiti and the administration has been pushing hard to recruit troops to join America to oust Haiti's military dictatorship and the Haiti leaders have announced that They would counter Act the foreign aggression. The petitioner further staled that the decision was taken during the Autum Session of the Jatiya Sangsad (parliament) to join" US led invasion" without the assent of the parliament and during the boycott of the Parliament by the leaders of the opposition parties. The petitioner also alleged that the decision is against the Fundamental Principle of State Policy and the Fundamental Rights as envisaged in our Constitution and for the decision to send troops of Bangladesh to participate in US-led war of aggression in Haiti there must exist a grave emergency to the satisfaction of the President that the security or economic life of Bangladesh of any part thereof is threatened by war or external aggression or internal disturbance.  Thus, the above quoted observations also support our view that extra-diction of Anup Chetia to India in no way violates Article 25 of our constitution as contended by the petitioner rather, if the Government extradict Anup Chetia to India it will be in consonance with the Fundamental Principles of State Policy and help base its international relations on the principles of respect for national sovereignty and equality, non-interference in the internal affairs of other countries. Now, it remains for us to consider the case cited from foreign jurisdiction. At the outset we must say that observations made therein are pious expression to secure international fundamental human right norms obtaining in different declarations and covenants of different stale parties to such instrument and have little binding 'force of the municipal Courts. Such views no doubt have opened a new horizon of International Human Right law but in international human rights law interpretation adopted by national courts can at best only be persuasive authority. In Ramoz Vs. DIAZ, the right of a foreign power to demand the extra diction was created by treaty. And in U.S. in absence of statutory of treaty provision no authority exits in the Government to surrender a fugitive criminal to a foreign Government. A careful reading of the judgment will show that the decision rests on Article VI of the treaty of Extra-diction made between Government of the U.S. and the Government of Cuba. Article VI of the treaty exempts extradition of a fugitive charged with political offence from the treaty. But Extra-diction Act, 1974 of our country does not provide such exemption. Therefore, the decision which is only of a persuasive value and decided placing reliance upon Article VI of the Extra-diction Treaty has no manner of application to the facts of the instant case. Let us now examine the contention whether in absence of any extra-diction treaty between Bangladesh and the Union of India the Government cans extradic Anup Chetia to India. In this regard relevant law is to be found in Section 4 of the Extra-diction Act, 1974 of Bangladesh Section 4 reads:- 

 7. Now let us consider Section 3(1) of the Special Powers Act, 1974. Section 3(1) of the Act empowers the Government to make an order directing any person to remove himself form Bangladesh in such a manner as it may specify in the order in order to prevent him from doing any prejudicial Act. Section 2(t) has given Meaning of the expression "prejudicial Act" According to Section 2(1) (I I) "prejudicial Act", amongst other, means Act to prejudice the maintenance of friendly relations of Bangladesh with foreign States." Thus in a case where a citizen or a foreign country intends to stay in Bangladesh and if the Government is satisfied that extra-diction of such person is called for in order to maintain friendly relations of Bangladesh with foreign States the Government can on the strength of section 3 (1) and Section 2 (f) (II) of the special powers Act, 1974 extradict such citizen to his own country in absence of any extra-diction treaty between the Government of Bangladesh and such foreign states. Thus, reading section 4 of the Extra-diction Act, 1974 and section 3 (1) read with section 2(I) (11) together we hold that the Government of Bangladesh has sufficient legal authority to extradict Anup Chetia to India in response to the right of India to demand extra-diction of Anup Chetia.
